claims.claim: Suppression weakens the avoided memory and can eventually lead to forgetting.
claims.source: This process weakens the avoided memory and can eventually lead to forgetting (Küpper et al., 2014; Stramaccia et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: There is little evidence for the neural consequences that underlie the sustained subsequent changes in the retrievability of a suppressed memory.
claims.source: Although this research has made strides in elucidating the transient mechanisms engaged during retrieval suppression (Anderson and Hanslmayr, 2014; Benoit et al., 2015; Benoit et al., 2016; Benoit and Anderson, 2012; Depue et al., 2007; Gagnepain et al., 2014; Gagnepain et al., 2017; Mary et al., 2020; Paz-Alonso et al., 2013), there is little evidence for the neural consequences that underlie the sustained subsequent changes in the retrievability of a suppressed memory.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature, identifying a gap in knowledge.

claims.claim: Successful episodic memory retrieval entails the reinstatement of a memory's representation.
claims.source: Successful episodic memory retrieval entails the reinstatement of a memory's representation (Frankland et al., 2019; Linde-Domingo et al., 2019; Tonegawa et al., 2015; Wing et al., 2015; Xue et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on memory retrieval.

claims.claim: Memory retrieval is fostered by hippocampal processes that complete the neural pattern from a partial pattern provided by a retrieval cue.
claims.source: It is fostered by hippocampal processes that complete the neural pattern of the original experience (e.g. of a particular scene) from a partial pattern provided by an adequate retrieval cue (e.g. of an object that was also part of the scene) (Knierim and Neunuebel, 2016; Liu et al., 2012; Neunuebel and Knierim, 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on hippocampal function.

claims.claim: Pattern completion leads to cortical reinstatement of a memory across regions involved in its original encoding.
claims.source: This process leads to the cortical reinstatement of a memory across the regions that had been involved in its original encoding (Grande et al., 2019; Horner et al., 2015; Rissman and Wagner, 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Successful retrieval has been shown to be accompanied by reactivation of categorical information that is widely distributed.
claims.source: Successful retrieval (e.g. of a particular scene) has thus been shown to be accompanied by a reactivation of categorical information (e.g. scene information) that is both widely distributed (Cooper and Ritchey, 2019; King et al., 2015; Rissman and Wagner, 2012; Wing et al., 2015) and localized to specific brain regions (e.g. the PhC; Martin et al., 2013; Staresina et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Successful retrieval has been shown to be accompanied by reactivation of categorical information localized to specific brain regions like the PhC.
claims.source: Successful retrieval (e.g. of a particular scene) has thus been shown to be accompanied by a reactivation of categorical information (e.g. scene information) that is both widely distributed (Cooper and Ritchey, 2019; King et al., 2015; Rissman and Wagner, 2012; Wing et al., 2015) and localized to specific brain regions (e.g. the PhC; Martin et al., 2013; Staresina et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: The degree of scene evidence on a given trial scaled with the vividness with which a memory could be retrieved.
claims.source: In the current study, the degree of scene evidence on a given trial scaled with the vividness with which a memory could be retrieved.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study's data analysis.

claims.claim: This extends prior evidence showing that PhC activation is stronger when scenes are recollected more vividly and in greater detail.
claims.source: This extends prior evidence showing that activation, particularly in the PhC, is stronger when scenes are recollected more vividly and in greater detail (Kensinger et al., 2011; Qin et al., 2011; Sheldon and Levine, 2013; Tendolkar et al., 2008; Todd et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim connects the current findings to prior research, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Intentional attempts to prevent retrieval led to reduced scene reactivation across the grey matter.
claims.source: We expected that intentional attempts to prevent retrieval should lead to reduced scene reactivation. This was the case in the current study across the grey matter as well as for the left PhC (see also Detre et al., 2013; Gagnepain et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study's data analysis.

claims.claim: Intentional attempts to prevent retrieval led to reduced scene reactivation in the left PhC.
claims.source: We expected that intentional attempts to prevent retrieval should lead to reduced scene reactivation. This was the case in the current study across the grey matter as well as for the left PhC (see also Detre et al., 2013; Gagnepain et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study's data analysis.

claims.claim: Suppression does not only affect the objective availability of a memory in an all-or-none fashion.
claims.source: This finding adds to the extant literature by showing that suppression does not only affect the objective availability of a memory in an all-or-none fashion (Stramaccia et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the current findings in relation to prior research.

claims.claim: By reducing vividness, suppression gradually diminishes the subjective quality of information that can be retrieved.
claims.source: By reducing the vividness of the memories, it also gradually diminishes the subjective quality of the information that can be retrieved.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the current findings.

claims.claim: Graded forgetting can be beneficial when it allows for continued conscious access to an aversive past event while dampening its affective impact.
claims.source: Such graded forgetting can be beneficial, for example when it allows for the continued conscious access to an aversive past event while dampening its affective impact (Norby et al., 2010; Visser et al., 2018, see also Cooper and Ritchey, 2019; Parks and Yonelinas, 2007; Richter et al., 2016a, for dissociations of retrieval success versus vividness).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: The sustained fading of a suppressed memory has been argued to result from deterioration of its neural representation.
claims.source: Critically, the sustained fading of a suppressed memory has been argued to result from a deterioration of its neural representation (Anderson and Hanslmayr, 2014; Depue, 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claims.claim: Deterioration of neural representations would lower the potential of these representations to be reinstated on later retrieval attempts.
claims.source: This deterioration, in turn, would lower the potential of these representations to be reinstated on later retrieval attempts.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on logical inference.

claims.claim: The classifier analysis yielded evidence for a greater reduction of scene reactivation for suppressed than baseline memories globally across the grey matter.
claims.source: The classifier analysis yielded evidence for a greater reduction of scene reactivation for suppressed than for baseline memories. This was the case at a global level across the grey matter as well as locally in the PhC.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the classifier analysis.

claims.claim: The classifier analysis yielded evidence for a greater reduction of scene reactivation for suppressed than baseline memories locally in the PhC.
claims.source: The classifier analysis yielded evidence for a greater reduction of scene reactivation for suppressed than for baseline memories. This was the case at a global level across the grey matter as well as locally in the PhC.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the classifier analysis.

claims.claim: Participants who displayed a greater suppression-induced reduction in scene reactivation in right PhC also experienced a greater reduction in vividness.
claims.source: Moreover, consistent with the contribution of the PhC to mnemonic vividness (Todd et al., 2013), participants who displayed a greater suppression-induced reduction in scene reactivation in the right PhC also experienced a greater reduction in vividness.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis.

claims.claim: Disruptions of cortical memory representations, such as in the PhC, may particularly lead to graded effects of forgetting.
claims.source: Indeed, disruptions of cortical memory representations, such as in the PhC, may particularly lead to these graded effects of forgetting (Gagnepain et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by a citation.

claims.claim: As cortical representations get progressively weakened, they may become increasingly susceptible to interference from overlapping representations of similar memories.
claims.source: That is, as cortical representations get progressively weakened, they may become increasingly susceptible to interference from overlapping representations of similar memories (Andermane et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Hippocampal representations are encoded in a more orthogonal fashion and may be largely protected from interference.
claims.source: By comparison, hippocampal representations are encoded in a more orthogonal fashion (Knierim and Neunuebel, 2016; Kumaran et al., 2016) and may thus be largely protected from interference.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by citations.

claims.claim: Disruption of hippocampal representations would not manifest as graded forgetting but eventually lead to holistic forgetting in an all-or-none fashion.
claims.source: The disruption of these representations would thus not manifest as graded forgetting but eventually lead to holistic forgetting in an all-or-none fashion (Andermane et al., 2021; Horner et al., 2015; Richter et al., 2016b).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by citations.

claims.claim: A previous study did not obtain evidence for lingering effects of suppression on hippocampal reinstatement when memories could still be recalled.
claims.source: Indeed, a previous study did not obtain evidence for lingering effects of suppression on hippocampal reinstatement when the memories could still be recalled (Liu et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: A pattern classifier is a powerful tool for inferring the reactivation of category-specific neural representations.
claims.source: A pattern classifier is a powerful tool for inferring the reactivation of category-specific neural representations (Haynes, 2015; Kuhl et al., 2012; Norman et al., 2006; Polyn et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior methodological research.

claims.claim: A pattern classifier does not provide evidence for the reinstatement of individual exemplars from within a category.
claims.source: As a downside, it does not provide evidence for the reinstatement of individual exemplars from within a category.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the method, based on methodological knowledge.

claims.claim: The retrieval of a memory should reinstate its representation, leading to similar activity patterns for a given memory on pre- and post-test.
claims.source: Specifically, given that the retrieval of a memory should reinstate its representation, we expected similar activity patterns to emerge for a given memory on the pre- and on the post-test (Danker et al., 2017; Staresina et al., 2012; Wing et al., 2015; Xue, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical prediction supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: For the baseline condition, activity patterns were more similar for the comparison of a memory with itself than with other memories.
claims.source: This was the case for the baseline condition, where the activity patterns were more similar for the comparison of a memory with itself than with the other memories.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the RSA analysis.

claims.claim: Reinstatement was not significant for suppressed memories.

claims.evidence: This is a finding from the RSA analysis.

claims.claim: The study did not obtain critical evidence that reinstatement was weaker for suppressed than baseline memories.
claims.source: However, we did not obtain the critical evidence that it was weaker than the baseline effect.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the RSA analysis.

claims.claim: The absence of a significant difference might reflect lower power for the more fine-grained analysis of individual activity patterns than for the more generic classifier.
claims.source: The absence of a significant difference in our study might simply reflect lower power for the more fine-grained, condition-rich analysis of individual activity patterns than for the more generic classifier (Nili et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the null finding, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The absence of a significant difference may result from repetition of identical objects as retrieval cues during pre- and post-tests.
claims.source: It may also result from the repetition of the identical objects as retrieval cues during the pre- and post-tests.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the null finding.

claims.claim: Right parahippocampal reinstatement was particularly affected in people who experienced the strongest decline in vividness.
claims.source: However, the absence of an overall effect might also reflect the varying degrees to which participants were successful at suppression (see also Appendix 1—table 1). Indeed, right parahippocampal reinstatement was particularly affected in those people who also experienced the strongest decline in vividness.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis.

claims.claim: The two sets of analyses converge in their support of the hypothesis that suppression leads to a sustained reduction in neural reinstatement.
claims.source: Together, the two sets of analyses thus converge in their support of our hypothesis that suppression leads to a sustained reduction in neural reinstatement.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined findings of the classifier and RSA analyses.

results.result: The study employed an adapted Think/No-Think procedure where participants learned object-scene associations, then underwent fMRI scanning during suppression and recall phases, with baseline items serving as controls for passive memory decay.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C35 describe the experimental design comprehensively. The procedure includes appropriate controls (baseline condition), counterbalancing, and clear operational definitions of conditions. The design is well-suited to test the stated hypotheses about sustained effects of suppression.

results.result: During the suppression phase, participants showed increased dlPFC activation and decreased hippocampal and parahippocampal activation during suppress versus recall trials, consistent with prior research on retrieval suppression mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C38 and C41-C44 report standard univariate fMRI findings that replicate established patterns in the literature. The statistical analyses appear appropriate and the findings are consistent with the cited prior work (C44), providing validation that the suppression manipulation was effective.

results.result: Suppression caused a reduction in self-reported memory vividness from pre- to post-test that exceeded changes in baseline memories, with this effect replicating across both an fMRI study (n=33) and an independent behavioral study (n=30).
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C53 present converging behavioral evidence from two independent samples with appropriate statistical tests (repeated measures ANOVAs, follow-up t-tests). The replication strengthens confidence in the behavioral effect. However, C47 and C52 show some inconsistency in baseline effects across studies, though the critical suppress vs. baseline interaction is consistent.

results.result: A pattern classifier trained to distinguish intact versus morphed aversive scenes achieved 80.3% accuracy globally and 77-83% accuracy in parahippocampal cortices, with greater scene reactivation correlating with more vivid recollections.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C59 establish the validity of the classifier approach. The cross-validation accuracies are significantly above chance (all p<.001) and the correlation with behavioral vividness ratings (C58-C59) provides important construct validity. This validates the use of classifier output as a proxy for memory reactivation.

results.result: During active suppression, scene reactivation was reduced globally across the brain (d=1.22) and locally in left parahippocampal cortex (d=0.50), but not in right parahippocampal cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C62 demonstrate transient effects of suppression on neural reactivation with large effect sizes and appropriate statistics. The lateralization (left but not right PhC) is interesting but unexplained. This provides evidence for the immediate neural consequences of suppression attempts.

results.result: Suppression led to sustained reductions in scene reactivation from pre- to post-test for suppressed but not baseline memories, both globally across grey matter and locally in parahippocampal cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C68 and C100-C101 provide the key evidence for sustained neural effects. The time × condition interactions are significant with appropriate effect sizes. The parallel findings at global and local levels strengthen the conclusion. This is central to the paper's main hypothesis about lasting neural consequences of suppression.

results.result: Greater suppression-induced reductions in parahippocampal scene reactivation were associated with greater reductions in memory vividness, significantly in right PhC (r=0.46) and trending in left PhC (r=0.34).
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 and C102 establish a critical link between neural and behavioral effects using robust correlation methods. The significant correlation in right PhC provides evidence that reduced reactivation underlies the phenomenological changes. The use of robust skipped correlations is appropriate given potential outliers in neuroimaging data.

results.result: There was no evidence for a relationship between sustained suppression-induced reductions in PhC scene evidence and transient deactivation during suppression.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72 report null findings with appropriate statistics and confidence intervals. While negative results, they are important for understanding the mechanisms - suggesting that sustained effects may not simply reflect the magnitude of transient suppression. The wide confidence intervals indicate uncertainty rather than evidence of absence.

results.result: Control regions (amygdala, V1, precuneus, angular gyrus) did not show sustained reductions in scene evidence following suppression, nor correlations with vividness changes, supporting the specificity of parahippocampal effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C75 and C82-C83 provide important specificity controls. The lack of effects in control regions strengthens the interpretation that PhC is particularly sensitive to suppression-induced changes. However, the control regions were selected post-hoc and the analyses are exploratory, limiting strong conclusions about regional specificity.

results.result: Representational similarity analysis showed significant memory-specific reinstatement for baseline memories but only a non-significant trend for suppressed memories, though the critical interaction between condition and reinstatement was not significant.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C79 and C111-C113 present RSA findings that partially support the hypothesis but lack the critical statistical interaction (C77, C113). The pattern is suggestive (baseline: p=.003, suppress: p=.075) but the failure to obtain a significant condition × identity interaction limits strong conclusions. The authors appropriately acknowledge this limitation.

results.result: Individual differences in suppression-induced reductions in vividness correlated with reductions in right parahippocampal reinstatement (r=0.39), with the two analytical approaches (classifier and RSA) converging to support sustained reductions in neural reinstatement.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C81 and C116-C117 show that despite the lack of a main effect in RSA, individual differences analyses reveal the predicted relationship in right PhC. This convergence between classifier and RSA approaches (C117) strengthens confidence in the sustained neural effects, though the RSA evidence is weaker than the classifier evidence.

results.result: The absence of a significant RSA interaction may reflect lower statistical power for fine-grained pattern analysis or confounding effects from repeated object cues.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C115 offer post-hoc explanations for null findings. While plausible (C114 is supported by citation), these remain speculative interpretations. The repeated cue issue (C115) is a legitimate methodological concern that could affect interpretation of same-item similarity, though it would affect both conditions equally.

results.result: Univariate analysis showed few regions with stronger pre-to-post decreases in activation for suppressed versus baseline memories, including parts of bilateral hippocampus.
results.evaluation: Claim C54 reports limited univariate effects, which is appropriate given that the study's hypotheses focus on multivariate pattern information. The finding of some hippocampal effects is consistent with the broader literature but is not central to the paper's main conclusions.

results.result: The study supports the hypothesis that suppression weakens memories by causing sustained deterioration of neural representations, which hinders subsequent reactivation and reduces the vividness of recollection.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4 state the hypothesis, while C10, C139-C142 present the main conclusions. The supporting evidence includes: (1) behavioral reductions in vividness (C39-C53), (2) sustained reductions in neural reactivation (C63-C68), and (3) correlations between neural and behavioral effects (C69-C70, C80). However, the causal language ('causes') is stronger than warranted by correlational data. The mechanism remains somewhat speculative (C132).

results.result: The study has limitations including lack of intrusion monitoring, focus on declarative rather than emotional components, and inability to establish causal links between transient suppression mechanisms and sustained after-effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C138 appropriately acknowledge study limitations. These are honest assessments that help contextualize the findings. The lack of intrusion data (C133-C134) is particularly relevant given theoretical claims about progressive weakening (C132). The inability to establish causality (C138) is an important caveat for the mechanistic interpretations.

results.result: Whole-brain classifier analysis showed sustained effects even when excluding parahippocampal cortex, though the data are consistent with preferential PhC involvement in scene processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C119 address the specificity of effects. The finding that global effects persist without PhC (C118) indicates distributed changes, while C119 appropriately notes PhC's special role in scene processing. This balanced interpretation acknowledges both regional specificity and distributed effects.

results.result: Scene evidence on individual trials scaled with memory vividness, and intentional suppression attempts led to reduced scene reactivation across grey matter and in left parahippocampal cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C94 validate the classifier approach and demonstrate transient suppression effects. The trial-by-trial correlation with vividness (C91) is important for establishing that classifier output reflects meaningful memory processes. These findings extend prior work (C92) and replicate established transient effects (C93-C94).

results.result: Suppression produces graded forgetting by reducing memory vividness rather than only affecting objective availability in an all-or-none fashion, which may be beneficial for dampening affective impact while maintaining conscious access.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C97 present an important conceptual contribution about graded versus all-or-none forgetting. The data support graded effects (continuous vividness ratings show reductions rather than complete forgetting). However, C97's claim about benefits is more speculative and relies on citations rather than direct evidence from this study.

results.result: Disruptions of cortical representations in parahippocampal cortex may lead to graded forgetting through interference, while hippocampal representations may be protected from interference due to orthogonal encoding, leading to all-or-none forgetting.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C107 present a theoretical framework about regional differences in forgetting patterns. While supported by citations (C103-C107), this remains largely speculative relative to the current data. The study does not directly test predictions about interference or compare cortical versus hippocampal forgetting patterns. C107 cites relevant prior work but doesn't constitute direct evidence.

results.result: Computational models and prior research suggest suppression may work through moderate reactivation followed by targeted inhibition of active features, potentially involving dlPFC-mediated disruption of hippocampal retrieval and GABAergic mechanisms, consistent with non-monotonic plasticity principles.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C130 present an extensive theoretical framework drawing on computational modeling and prior research. While well-cited and conceptually coherent, these mechanisms are not directly tested in the current study. The integration with non-monotonic plasticity (C127-C128) is interesting but speculative. Claims C129-C130 about dlPFC's role are particularly speculative given the current data.
